title: Components
summary: The anatomy of an Angular component: decorator, selector, template, styles and class, how components nest, how styles are scoped and the lifecycle hooks you will actually use.
introduction: A component is the unit of Angular: a class that owns a piece of the page, the HTML that draws it and the styles that dress it. Every screen you build is a tree of components passing data down and events up. This lesson takes a component apart, shows how to use one inside another, explains why a component's CSS cannot leak into its neighbours, and introduces the two lifecycle hooks that most components need.
learningObjectives: Write a component with a selector, template, styles and state
Use a component inside another by importing it
Explain view encapsulation and when ngOnInit and ngOnDestroy run

blocks.text: Three things make a class a component: the `@Component` decorator, which carries the metadata; a **selector**, which is the tag name other templates use; and a **template**, which is the HTML Angular renders. The class holds the state and the methods the template calls.

items: `name` and `expanded` are signals, so the template updates when they change. `year` is a plain property; that works too, but Angular only knows it changed because the click handler ran, not because the value did.
`initials` is a `computed()`: a value derived from other signals that recalculates only when `name` changes.
`styles` holds CSS that applies to this component only (more on that below).
Methods called from the template, such as `toggle()`, are ordinary class methods.

blocks.text: `template` and `styles` keep everything in one file, which is ideal for small components. For larger ones use `templateUrl: './user-card.html'` and `styleUrl: './user-card.css'`; the paths are relative to the `.ts` file and `ng generate component` creates this layout by default. Angular compiles both forms identically, so choose by readability: once a template no longer fits on one screen, move it out.

A component can only use tags that it knows about. Add the child class to the parent's `imports` array, then write its selector in the template. Self-closing tags such as `<app-user-card />` are allowed for components.

blocks.text: Each `<app-user-card />` is a separate **instance** with its own signals: clicking *More* on the first card does not expand the second. Right now both cards show the same person because the data lives inside the component; the [inputs and outputs lesson](/tutorials/angular/inputs-outputs) shows how a parent passes different data to each child.

blocks.title: Common mistake: forgetting the import
blocks.text: Use `<app-user-card />` without adding `UserCard` to `imports` and the build fails with `NG8001: 'app-user-card' is not a known element`. The message continues with the fix: verify that the component is included in the `@Component.imports` of the parent. Every component, directive and pipe a template uses must be listed there.

blocks.text: The `h2` rule in `UserCard` does not affect the `<h1>` in `App`, nor any `<h2>` elsewhere. Angular's default **view encapsulation** (`Emulated`) adds a generated attribute such as `_ngcontent-ng-c123` to every element of the component's template and rewrites each selector to require it. Styles therefore apply only to the component's own elements, and global styles in `src/styles.css` still apply everywhere.

blocks.title: What the browser receives for the h2 rule

blocks.text: Two selectors are special. `:host` targets the component's own element (`<app-user-card>`), which is useful for `display: block` or a border around the whole component. `::ng-deep` punches through encapsulation to style children; it is deprecated and best avoided because it makes styles leak in exactly the way encapsulation prevents.

blocks.text: Angular creates a component, renders it, updates it as state changes and eventually destroys it. You can run code at these moments by implementing lifecycle hooks. Most components need at most two.

rows: When the class is instantiated, before inputs have values
Once, after the first inputs are set
Work that needs input values, such as starting a timer
Just before the component is removed
After the DOM has been written
Browser-only work such as measuring an element

blocks.title: src/app/clock/clock.ts
In the browser, after three seconds

blocks.text: The interval updates a signal, so the paragraph re-renders every second without any extra wiring. Clearing it in `ngOnDestroy` matters: a timer that outlives its component keeps running, updates state nobody displays and, if it holds a reference to the component, prevents garbage collection. Angular also offers `DestroyRef` for the same job inside services and functions: `inject(DestroyRef).onDestroy(() => clearInterval(timer))`.

blocks.title: Keep components small
blocks.text: A component that fetches data, filters it, renders a table and handles a form is four components waiting to be split. Small components with one job are easier to test, reuse and read; the [services lesson](/tutorials/angular/services-di) shows where the shared logic goes.

questions.question: Two `<app-user-card />` tags are rendered by the same parent. What happens when you click *More* on the first one?
questions.explanation: Each tag creates a separate instance with its own signals, so only the first card expands.
options: Angular throws an error because a component may be used only once

questions.question: A CSS rule in a component's `styles` applies to matching elements in every other component as well.
questions.explanation: With the default emulated encapsulation, component styles are rewritten to match only that component's elements. Global rules belong in `src/styles.css`.
